newsitem.title: BOSNIA: US envoy says Croats tolerate crime in Mostar.
newsitem.headline: US envoy says Croats tolerate crime in Mostar.

text.p: United States envoy Robert Gelbard accused Bosnian Croat authorities on Tuesday of refusing to integrate their police with their Moslem counterparts and tolerating drug trafficking and other crime.

Gelbard threatened to cut off U.S. aid to Mostar unless Croats made good on promises to reform their police force to represent both Croat and Moslem communities in the bitterly divided southern Bosnian town.
"Mostar today is considered the crime capital of Europe. Drug trafficking, stolen cars and contraband are frequently passing through Mostar," Gelbard told reporters.
"The question I have to ask is why don't the Croat authorities stop drug-traffickers and the other criminals? Why don't they want to stop the contraband?"
Gelbard said the only way to establish a "legitimate economy" in Mostar was to restructure the police on the basis of reforms set down by United Nations police monitors.
"We have heard too often the promises from the Croat authorities about their willingness to establish this police force, which they break immediately," he said.
"If they do not reach an acceptable agreement today...I will cut off all economic assistance to that area, within the capacity of the U.S. government."
Reforms proposed by the International Police Task Force (IPTF) are supposed to reduce the size of police departments and ensure forces reflect the etnic composition of Bosnian towns.

But Croat and Serb authorities have resisted the guidelines and only police in the Moslem-led Sarajevo canton have carried out the reforms, which require officers to wear identification badges and to submit to vetting by the IPTF.
Bosnian Croat leaders have also refused to form joint police patrols throughout the Mostar region and have opposed power-sharing agreements for the canton admnistration.

The stalemate over the Mostar police forced the postponement of a planned meeting this week between Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and the Moslem chairman of the Bosnian collective presidency, Alija Izetbegovic.
Izetbegovic has demanded that Croats in Mostar implement agreements on the joint police force before he meets Tudjman, the patron of the Bosnian Croats.
A 10-month war between Bosnian Croats and Moslems in 1993 devastated Mostar and left it divided into Croat and Moslem sectors.
Croat authorities in the western Herzegovnia region employ the currency and flag of neighbouring Croatia and oppose plans to allow Moslem or Serb refugees to move back.
